cards.title: Egress Pricing — The Silent Budget Killer
cards.teaser: Moving data into GCP is free. Moving data out is not. Egress charges are metered by destination, and they accumulate invisibly until the first billing cycle surprises a team that never thought to model them.

runs.text: GCP's pricing model, like all major cloud providers, follows an asymmetric pattern:
ingress is free, egress is billed.

This asymmetry reflects physical economics — bandwidth out of a data center has a cost; bandwidth in does not. The practical consequence is that architectures designed without awareness of egress traffic patterns routinely exceed their compute budget by 2-5x once real traffic flows.
Egress charges apply at several layers:

items.text: Data leaving GCP to the internet
— the most expensive tier, billed per GB with a tiered rate (the first TB/month is cheapest; subsequent tiers are progressively cheaper but the per-GB rate is still significant).
Data crossing GCP regions
— lower than internet egress but non-zero; east-west traffic between a us-central1 Cloud Run service and a europe-west1 Cloud SQL instance will accumulate charges.
Data crossing zones within a region
— typically cheaper still, but not free; a multi-zone GKE cluster where services are unaware of zone affinity can generate surprising intra-region egress.

runs.text: The FinOps community consistently identifies egress as the line item that most surprises teams at cloud maturity. The charge is metered at the network layer, so it does not appear in any per-service dashboard — it shows up as a single line in the Network section of the bill. Teams that only examine per-service costs miss it entirely.

Common egress traps: loading large GCS objects in a loop (each read is egress if the consumer is off-GCP), streaming Pub/Sub messages to an on-premises system, and returning large API responses to mobile clients from a Cloud Run service. Model the data flows before you architect — not after.

GCP charges you for data leaving, not arriving. The further the data travels — same region, different region, internet — the higher the per-GB rate. Most teams discover this on their second billing statement.

cards.title: Cross-Region Egress Within GCP
cards.teaser: Traffic between two GCP regions stays on Google's private backbone but is still billed. Intra-cloud cross-region egress is cheaper than internet egress but is a common source of invisible cost for multi-region architectures.

runs.text: A common misconception: because GCP owns its global fiber network, data transferred between regions must be free. It is not. GCP meters cross-region traffic and charges a per-GB rate that is lower than internet egress but accumulates quickly at scale.
The rate structure as of this writing (verify current pricing at cloud.google.com/vpc/network-pricing):

items.text: Same region, same zone
— free between VM instances; small charges may apply for managed services.
Same region, different zones
— charged per GB in both directions. This is the zone-to-zone egress that surprises teams running multi-zone Kubernetes clusters.
Different regions, same continent
— charged per GB; roughly half the internet egress rate.
Different regions, different continents
— higher per-GB rate; intercontinental traffic is the most expensive intra-cloud path.

runs.text: Architectural mitigations:

items.text: Topology-aware routing in GKE
— routes traffic to the nearest zone-local pod first, reducing inter-zone hops.
Regional endpoints for managed services
— use Cloud SQL, Firestore, and BigQuery in the same region as the services consuming them.
Caching with Cloud CDN or Memorystore
— serve repeated reads from cache co-located with consumers rather than fetching from a distant primary.

runs.text: GCP Network Intelligence Center includes a Network Topology view that visualizes traffic flows between regions and zones. Use it to identify cross-region data paths that may not be obvious from application architecture diagrams.

Even within GCP, traffic that hops between regions costs money. The charge is lower than internet egress, but multi-region architectures with chatty services can rack up significant intra-cloud egress bills.

cards.title: Internet Egress — The Expensive Tier
cards.teaser: Data leaving GCP and heading to the public internet is billed at the highest egress rate. Understanding the tiered pricing structure and the free-egress paths available (Cloud CDN, direct peering) materially reduces this cost for consumer-facing workloads.

runs.text: Internet egress — data flowing from GCP to any destination on the public internet — is metered by region of origin and by total monthly volume. Pricing is tiered: the first terabyte per month costs the most per GB; volumes above 10 TB/month benefit from progressively lower rates. Exact rates change; always check cloud.google.com/vpc/network-pricing for the current schedule.
Two legitimate paths to reduce or eliminate internet egress charges:

items.text: Cloud CDN egress discount

— traffic served from Cloud CDN edge PoPs is billed at the CDN egress rate, which is significantly lower than the standard internet egress rate. For static assets and cacheable API responses, fronting a Cloud Load Balancer with Cloud CDN can cut egress costs by 50-80%.
Google's direct peering and CDN interconnect

— ISPs and CDN providers that have established peering agreements with Google receive egress at preferential or zero rates. If a significant portion of your users are on networks with Google peering, effective egress costs are lower than the list rate.
Cloud Storage free egress to Google products
— data read from Cloud Storage by BigQuery or other GCP services within the same region incurs no egress charge. The free path requires same-region co-location.

runs.text: A practical FinOps heuristic: any workload that serves large objects (video, images, large API payloads) to end users should route through Cloud CDN by default. The CDN egress rate pays for the Cloud CDN cost and saves money at any meaningful volume. Teams that discover this after launch routinely wish they had designed it in from the start.

Cloud Storage buckets accessed directly by end users (not proxied via Cloud CDN or a load balancer) generate internet egress charges at the full rate. Serving public assets directly from a GCS bucket without a CDN layer is a reliable way to produce unexpectedly large egress bills.

Internet egress is the most expensive data movement in GCP. Cloud CDN cuts the rate substantially for cacheable content; co-locating consumers and storage within the same region avoids the charge entirely for intra-GCP flows.

cards.title: Per-Service Quotas
cards.teaser: Every GCP service has quotas — rate limits and resource caps applied per project, per region, or per user. Quotas prevent runaway workloads from monopolizing shared infrastructure, but they also become operational blockers when a legitimate workload grows beyond its default allocation.

runs.text: GCP quotas exist in two categories:

items.text: Rate quotas

— the number of API requests or operations allowed per unit of time. For example: Compute Engine API calls per minute, BigQuery queries per day, Cloud Spanner reads per second. Exceeding a rate quota returns a
429 RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED
error.
Allocation quotas

— the total quantity of a resource allowed to exist at any time. CPUs per region, IP addresses per project, persistent disk capacity. Exceeding an allocation quota prevents resource creation until the quota is raised or existing resources are deleted.

runs.text: Quotas are applied at multiple scopes:

items.text: Per project
— the most common scope. Each project starts with the default quota. Projects can be raised independently.
Per region
— resource quotas are often regional. A project may have 72 vCPUs available in us-central1 and a separate 72 vCPU quota in europe-west1.
Per user or service account
— some API quotas are per-caller, not per-project.

runs.text: The IAM Quotas page at console.google.com/iam-admin/quotas lists all quotas for the selected project, their current usage, and a button to request increases. The Quotas API also exposes this data programmatically, making it possible to alert on quota utilization before it becomes a production incident.

Quota exhaustion is a common cause of silent production failures. A service that depends on a GCP API will fail requests when the quota is exhausted, but may not surface this as a visible error in application logs without explicit handling of RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED responses. Treat quota utilization as a metric worth alerting on.

Every GCP service caps how fast you can call it and how much of it you can own. These caps protect everyone on the shared platform, but they will stop your workload cold if you hit them without planning ahead.

cards.title: Quota Increase Requests
cards.teaser: Default quotas are starting points, not ceilings. The process for requesting a quota increase is straightforward, but it takes time — requesting increases before hitting production limits is standard operational practice.

runs.text: The standard quota increase process:

items.text: Navigate to IAM & Admin > Quotas
in the Cloud Console, or use the Quotas API to find the quota you need raised.
Select the specific quota
— filter by service, region, and quota name. Many quota names are not intuitive; the console search helps.
Click Edit Quotas
and enter the new limit value with a justification. Google uses the justification to evaluate whether the request is legitimate and to size the approval.
Wait for approval

— small increases on widely-used services are often auto-approved within minutes. Large increases or increases on constrained services (e.g., GPU quota) may take 2-5 business days or require sales involvement.

runs.text: Operational best practices for quota management:

items.text: Request increases 2-4 weeks before a planned capacity event
— product launch, load test, seasonal peak. Do not wait until you hit the limit.
Set quota usage alerts at 70-80%
— Cloud Monitoring has a
serviceusage.googleapis.com/quota/usage
metric that can trigger alerts before exhaustion.
Separate projects for production and non-production
— each project has independent quotas. A load test in a staging project cannot exhaust production quotas.
Terraform-managed quota requests
— the
google_service_usage_consumer_quota_override
resource allows managing quota overrides as infrastructure code, making quota state auditable and reproducible.

runs.text: GPU and TPU quotas require specific justification and are not auto-approved. ML teams that discover GPU quota at zero when launching a training job face multi-day delays. Provision GPU quota in advance as part of project setup, even if the training jobs are weeks away.

To raise a quota: find it in the console, click Edit, enter a number and a reason, and wait. The wait can be minutes or days depending on the service. Always ask early — quota increases do not take effect retroactively.

cards.title: Committed-Use Discounts (CUDs)
cards.teaser: Committed-use discounts let you trade scheduling flexibility for price — commit to a baseline resource level for 1 or 3 years and pay 20-55% less than on-demand rates. Flex CUDs reduce the commitment risk for variable workloads.

runs.text: CUDs are GCP's mechanism for passing volume savings to customers willing to make a forward commitment. Two commitment types exist:

items.text: Resource-based CUDs

— commit to a specific number of vCPUs and GB of memory in a specific region for 1 or 3 years. Discounts are approximately 37% (1yr) and 55% (3yr) compared to on-demand pricing. Machine type does not need to be specified at commitment time — you commit to resource quantities and the discount applies to any machine family using those resources.
Spend-based CUDs

— commit to a minimum monthly spend (in dollars) on a specific service (e.g., Cloud Run, Cloud SQL). In exchange, GCP discounts usage above baseline at a preferential rate. Useful for services where resource units are not natural to reason about.

runs.text: Flex CUDs (introduced for Compute Engine) reduce the lock-in risk:

items.text: Smaller discount than standard CUDs
— approximately 20% vs 37%, in exchange for commitment to a shorter minimum term and the ability to cancel with a notice period.
Designed for growth-stage workloads
— teams that are scaling rapidly and cannot predict 1-3 year resource needs with confidence can still capture meaningful savings without locking in at the wrong level.

runs.text: CUD purchases are applied at the project or billing account level. GCP applies them automatically to eligible usage — you do not need to tag individual VMs. The Cloud Billing console shows CUD utilization; a commitment with low utilization is money wasted.

FinOps practitioners apply the 70% rule before recommending a CUD purchase: if a workload runs at or above its baseline for at least 70% of the time, a CUD is almost certainly net-positive. Below 70%, the commitment may cost more than on-demand if usage drops. Use Billing Export to BigQuery to measure actual utilization before committing.

A CUD is a promise to use a certain amount of GCP for 1 or 3 years in exchange for a 20-55% discount. Flex CUDs offer a smaller discount with lower commitment risk. Commit to what you are confident you will use; cover variable capacity with on-demand or spot.

cards.title: Sustained-Use Discounts
cards.teaser: Sustained-use discounts (SUDs) are automatic — no commitment required. GCP progressively discounts Compute Engine instances that run for more than 25% of a calendar month, reaching up to 30% off at 100% utilization.

runs.text: Sustained-use discounts are GCP's most distinctive pricing feature. Unlike AWS Reserved Instances or Azure Reserved VM Instances, SUDs require no upfront commitment, no minimum term, and no configuration. They are calculated automatically at billing time.
How SUD calculation works:

items.text: 0-25% of the month
— full on-demand rate (no discount).
25-50% of the month
— approximately 20% discount on the incremental usage in this band.
50-75% of the month
— approximately 40% discount on the incremental usage in this band.
75-100% of the month
— approximately 60% discount on the incremental usage in this band.

runs.text: The blended effective discount for an instance that runs the full month is approximately 30% off the on-demand rate. SUDs apply to General Purpose (N1, N2, N2D) and Memory-Optimized (M1, M2) machine families. They do not apply to preemptible/spot VMs, Autopilot GKE, Cloud Run, or App Engine.
CUD vs SUD trade-off:

items.text: SUD
— automatic, no commitment, ~30% effective discount at full-month utilization. Best for steady workloads where you want savings without commitment risk.
CUD (1yr)
— requires commitment, ~37% discount. Beats SUD for baseline usage you are confident will persist.
CUD (3yr)
— ~55% discount. Best for stable, well-understood baseline. SUDs and CUDs stack: CUD covers the baseline; SUD covers overflow that exceeds the CUD commitment.

runs.text: SUDs are calculated per machine type prefix, not per individual VM. GCP combines usage across all VMs of the same type within a project and region before calculating the discount. This means that spinning up and tearing down many small VMs throughout the month accumulates SUD credit as if it were a single steady VM.

Sustained-use discounts are free money for running VMs steadily — GCP gives you up to 30% off automatically for any Compute Engine instance that runs more than a quarter of the month. No sign-up required.

cards.title: The Free Tier — Always-Free and the $300 Trial
cards.teaser: GCP has two free-tier mechanisms: a 90-day $300 trial credit for new accounts, and a permanent always-free tier for small workloads. Knowing exactly what is always-free prevents charges from appearing when trial credits expire.

runs.text: The two tiers serve different purposes:

items.text: $300 trial credit (90 days)

— available to new GCP accounts. The credit expires after 90 days or when exhausted, whichever comes first. All GCP services are accessible during the trial (with some limits on GPU and high-quota resources). The trial is the primary way teams prototype new architectures before committing budget.
Always-free tier
— permanent monthly allowances that do not expire and apply regardless of whether a trial is active. Always-free limits are per billing account, not per project.

runs.text: Key always-free tier allocations (verify at cloud.google.com/free — limits change):

items.text: Compute Engine
— one e2-micro VM instance per month in us-west1, us-central1, or us-east1; 30 GB of standard persistent disk.
Cloud Storage
— 5 GB of regional storage in US regions; 1 GB of egress per month to North America.
Cloud Functions
— 2 million invocations per month; 400,000 GB-seconds of compute time.
Cloud Run
— 2 million requests per month; 360,000 vCPU-seconds; 180,000 GB-seconds.
BigQuery
— 10 GB of storage per month; 1 TB of query data processed per month.
Firestore
— 1 GB of storage; 50,000 reads, 20,000 writes, 20,000 deletes per day.
Pub/Sub
— 10 GB of messages per month.

runs.text: The trial credit masks real costs. Teams building on GCP with $300 in trial credit often discover significant bills the month after the trial expires. Model what the workload would cost without the trial credit before launch. The GCP Pricing Calculator at cloud.google.com/products/calculator is the right tool for this exercise.

New GCP accounts get $300 to spend over 90 days. After that, the always-free tier provides small permanent allowances on popular services — but the amounts are modest. Do not design a production workload around the always-free limits.

cards.title: Billing Exports to BigQuery
cards.teaser: Cloud Billing can stream every billing record to a BigQuery dataset in near-real time. This is the foundation of serious FinOps work — without the raw billing data in a queryable store, cost analysis is limited to the Cloud Console's pre-built charts.

runs.text: The Cloud Console billing view provides aggregated summaries but does not support ad-hoc analysis. Enabling billing export to BigQuery gives you a raw, row-level dataset where every charge — down to the sub-cent resource usage line — is queryable with SQL.
Two export types are available:

items.text: Standard usage cost export
— daily-granularity records for all billable usage. Sufficient for trend analysis and cost attribution.
Detailed usage cost export
— includes resource-level labels and is refreshed more frequently. Required for workload-level cost attribution using Billing labels.

runs.text: Example BigQuery queries used by FinOps teams:

items.text: Top 10 services by cost last 30 days:

explanation.text:
SELECT
  service.description AS service,
  ROUND(SUM(cost), 2) AS total_cost_usd
FROM `my-billing-project.billing_export.gcp_billing_export_v1_XXXXXX`
WHERE DATE(usage_start_time) >= DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 30 DAY)
GROUP BY service
ORDER BY total_cost_usd DESC
LIMIT 10;

items.text: Egress cost breakdown by SKU:

explanation.text:
SELECT
  sku.description AS sku,
  SUM(usage.amount) AS total_bytes,
  ROUND(SUM(cost), 2) AS total_cost_usd
FROM `my-billing-project.billing_export.gcp_billing_export_v1_XXXXXX`
WHERE DATE(usage_start_time) >= DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 7 DAY)
  AND LOWER(sku.description) LIKE '%egress%'
GROUP BY sku
ORDER BY total_cost_usd DESC;

runs.text: Enable the export in Cloud Console > Billing > Billing Export > BigQuery Export. Data begins flowing within 24 hours; historical data before the export was enabled is not backfilled.

The Looker Studio (formerly Data Studio) community has pre-built billing dashboards that connect directly to the BigQuery billing export dataset. Importing one of these templates is a fast path to an organization-wide cost visibility dashboard without writing SQL from scratch.

Billing export to BigQuery turns your GCP invoice into a SQL database. Every dollar is a row. You can query, group, and join it against your own data — that is how FinOps teams answer questions like "which team owns the largest egress spend" or "how much does our nightly batch job cost."

cards.title: Budget Alerts
cards.teaser: Cloud Billing budgets let you define a spend threshold and receive notifications — or trigger automated responses — when GCP usage approaches or exceeds it. Budget alerts are the minimum viable spend guardrail for any production project.

runs.text: A Cloud Billing budget is configured per billing account or per project, with an optional service or label filter. It fires notifications when cumulative spend in the current calendar month crosses defined threshold percentages.
Budget alert configuration (via Cloud Console or Terraform):
Two alert paths:

items.text: Email notifications
— sent to billing account administrators and optionally to Cloud Monitoring notification channels (email, Slack via webhook, PagerDuty). Suitable for awareness alerts.
Pub/Sub notifications

— the budget fires a message to a Pub/Sub topic, which can trigger a Cloud Function to take automated action: disable billing on the project, send a Slack message with a breakdown, or create an incident ticket. This is the programmatic path for enforcing hard spend limits.

runs.text: Important nuances:

items.text: Budget alerts do not stop spending
— they only notify. Disabling billing via a Cloud Function is the only automated way to cap spend, and it will break the application.
Forecasted spend threshold
— the
FORECASTED_SPEND
basis triggers the alert when GCP's projection of month-end spend crosses the threshold, even if current spend has not. Useful for catching spend spikes early in the month.

runs.text: Budget alerts lag by up to 24 hours — GCP billing data is not real-time. A sudden spike from a runaway job (e.g., a BigQuery query scanning petabytes without a cost control) may generate a large charge before the alert fires. Use per-query cost controls (BigQuery maximum bytes billed) in addition to budget alerts.

A budget alert is a notification that says "you have spent X% of your planned amount this month." It can email you, ping Slack, or trigger a Cloud Function to take action. It does not stop the spending — it just tells you it is happening.

cards.title: Active Assist Cost Recommendations
cards.teaser: Active Assist is GCP's AI-driven recommendation engine. Its cost recommenders analyze your actual usage patterns and surface specific, actionable savings opportunities — idle VM recommendations, oversized disk recommendations, and CUD purchase recommendations — without requiring manual analysis.

runs.text: Active Assist operates as a set of recommenders — each one specialized for a particular service and cost pattern. Recommendations are surfaced in the Cloud Console under each service's overview, in the Recommender API, and in the Active Assist console (console.cloud.google.com/active-assist).
Key cost recommenders:

items.text: Idle VM recommender

— identifies Compute Engine instances with very low CPU and network utilization over the past 14 days. Recommendation: stop or delete. These are typically forgotten development VMs or over-provisioned batch machines.
VM rightsizing recommender
— analyzes CPU and memory utilization and suggests downsizing to a smaller machine type. The recommendation includes estimated savings and projected performance impact.
Idle persistent disk recommender
— finds persistent disks not attached to any VM (orphaned disks from deleted instances). These continue billing at full price indefinitely.
Idle IP address recommender
— reserved static IPs not attached to any resource are billed continuously. This recommender surfaces them for release.
CUD recommender
— analyzes project-level Compute Engine usage and recommends specific CUD purchases sized to match stable baseline usage. Includes estimated annual savings.
Cloud SQL instance recommender
— identifies oversized or idle Cloud SQL instances based on query volume and connection patterns.

runs.text: Integrating Active Assist into operations:

items.text: Recommender API
— programmatically fetch recommendations and route them to Jira tickets or Slack channels. Teams that automate recommendation triage are significantly more likely to act on them.
Weekly review cadence

— FinOps practitioners recommend a weekly 15-minute review of new recommendations as part of the engineering cycle. Recommendations expire after 90 days of inaction; acting on them promptly captures savings sooner.

runs.text: Active Assist recommendations can be dismissed, acknowledged, or claimed. Dismissed recommendations are hidden and tracked; this audit trail is useful for compliance and for distinguishing "we reviewed and chose not to act" from "we never looked at it."

Active Assist watches your GCP usage and tells you specifically where you are wasting money — an idle VM here, an orphaned disk there, a CUD you should buy. It does the detective work; you just have to act on it.

cards.title: Cloud Billing Labels
cards.teaser: Billing labels are key-value tags attached to GCP resources that flow through to the billing export. They are the primary mechanism for cost allocation — attributing spend to teams, products, environments, or cost centers from a single billing account.

runs.text: A GCP label is a key-value pair (e.g.,
team=platform
env=production
cost-center=eng-123

) attached to a resource at creation time or updated later. Labels on resources propagate to the billing export, where they appear as columns in the BigQuery table, enabling SQL-based cost attribution.
Effective labeling strategy:

items.text: Define a label taxonomy before provisioning resources
— retroactively labeling existing resources is painful. Common dimensions:
env
(production/staging/dev),
team
service
(the application name),
cost-center
(for finance attribution).
Enforce labels via Organization Policy
— the
gcp.resourceLocations
constraint and custom Organization Policies can require labels on resource creation. Without enforcement, label coverage degrades over time.
Infrastructure-as-code default labels
— Terraform modules that provision resources should include a
labels
variable with required keys defaulted to module-level context (team, environment). This makes labeling the path of least resistance.

runs.text: Querying cost by label in BigQuery:

explanation.text:
SELECT
  (SELECT value FROM UNNEST(labels) WHERE key = 'team') AS team,
  (SELECT value FROM UNNEST(labels) WHERE key = 'env') AS env,
  ROUND(SUM(cost), 2) AS total_cost_usd
FROM `my-billing-project.billing_export.gcp_billing_export_v1_XXXXXX`
WHERE DATE(usage_start_time) >= DATE_SUB(CURRENT_DATE(), INTERVAL 30 DAY)
GROUP BY team, env
ORDER BY total_cost_usd DESC;

runs.text: Label limitations to be aware of:

items.text: Not all GCP resources support labels
— some managed services (certain network primitives, Cloud Identity) do not propagate labels to billing. Verify label support for each service you provision.
Label changes do not backfill billing data
— adding a label today only affects billing records from today forward.
Maximum of 64 labels per resource
— not a practical constraint for most teams, but worth knowing.

runs.text: The FinOps Foundation's tagging/labeling guidance recommends treating labels as a contract between engineering and finance: engineering commits to labeling resources consistently; finance commits to using label data for chargeback and showback reports rather than requiring per-project billing accounts. This division of responsibility scales better than one-project-per-team structures.

Billing labels are key-value tags on resources that flow into the billing export. They let you answer "how much did the checkout service cost in production last month" by querying BigQuery instead of guessing. No labels means no cost attribution.

cards.title: CUD Recommendations — Rightsizing Commit Purchases
cards.teaser: Buying the wrong CUD is worse than buying none: over-committing wastes money on capacity you will not use; under-committing leaves discount on the table. Active Assist's CUD recommender analyzes actual usage to size commitments correctly.

runs.text: The CUD recommender in Active Assist is distinct from the general cost recommendations. It specifically analyzes Compute Engine vCPU and memory consumption across a project over a 30-day lookback window and produces a commitment recommendation sized to match the stable baseline.
What the recommendation includes:

items.text: Commitment type
— resource-based (vCPU + memory) or spend-based (dollars per month), the commitment term (1yr or 3yr), and the specific machine family to target.
Projected savings
— estimated annual savings compared to the on-demand rate, accounting for SUDs already applied.
Confidence level
— high, medium, or low, based on how stable the usage pattern is. Low-confidence recommendations deserve more scrutiny before committing.

runs.text: Practical approach to CUD purchases using the recommender:

items.text: Start with a 1yr commitment on high-confidence recommendations
— the 3yr rate is better, but the 1yr commitment leaves room to adjust if the architecture changes.
Cover 80% of stable baseline with CUDs, leave 20% for SUDs
— this ratio accounts for occasional usage drops without wasting the commitment. SUDs cover the remainder automatically.
Review recommendations quarterly
— as projects grow or shrink, the optimal CUD level changes. The recommender updates continuously; quarterly reviews align CUD purchases with current usage reality.
Use billing account-level CUDs for organizations with multiple projects

— billing account-level commitments apply across all projects, allowing surplus from one project to offset usage in another. This is the appropriate scope for organizations rather than per-project commitments.

runs.text: CUD utilization is reported in the Cloud Billing console under Committed Use Discounts. A utilization consistently below 70% indicates the commitment was oversized. The recommender will surface a "reduce commitment" signal in the next recommendation cycle, though you cannot reduce an existing commitment — only choose not to renew it.

The CUD recommender looks at how much compute you actually ran over the past month and tells you exactly what commitment to buy to get the maximum discount without over-committing. It does the math; you just need to review and click purchase.
